title: Order the snapshot-based migration workflow
description: From entity change to merged PR — the eight steps of MikroORM's snapshot-based migration workflow. Drop them in the right order.

widgetConfig.prompt: Order the steps from 'developer edits an entity' to 'CI green, PR mergeable'.

steps.label: 1. Edit the entity: add a slug field to Book.
2. Run `npx mikro-orm migration:create --name=add_slug_to_book`.
steps.detail: MikroORM diffs the entity model against .snapshot-*.json, NOT against the live DB.

steps.label: 3. Open the generated migration file and review the up() / down() bodies.
steps.detail: Hand-edit if a backfill SQL is needed before the column becomes NOT NULL.

steps.label: 4. Commit BOTH the migration file AND the regenerated .snapshot-*.json.
steps.detail: The snapshot is the new 'baseline' the next migration will diff against.

steps.label: 5. Test locally: drop the local DB or run `migration:fresh`, then `migration:up`.
steps.detail: Skipping this is how 'relation already exists' bites a teammate.

steps.label: 6. CI runs migration:check — must pass with zero diff against the entities (proves no drift).
7. On deploy, run migration:up BEFORE the new service code starts.
8. Start the new service code that depends on the new column.

modelAnswer: Edit -> generate -> hand-review -> commit the snapshot too -> verify locally on a clean DB -> CI guards against drift -> migration runs before the service code -> service starts. Two non-obvious steps: committing the snapshot (forgetting it is the #1 way teams diverge), and running the migration BEFORE the new service code (otherwise the new code crashes against the old schema).

title: Reorder the shuffled migration file body
description: Below is a real migration up() body for 'add slug to book' — but the lines are shuffled. Drag them into the correct execution order.

widgetConfig.prompt: Reorder the lines so the migration: (1) adds the slug column nullable first, (2) backfills slugs from existing titles, (3) makes the column NOT NULL, (4) adds the unique constraint. This is the safe zero-downtime ordering the lesson hammers.
lines: this.addSql(`alter table "book" add column "slug" varchar(255) null;`);
this.addSql(`update "book" set "slug" = lower(replace("title", ' ', '-')) where "slug" is null;`);
this.addSql(`alter table "book" alter column "slug" set not null;`);

modelAnswer: Add the column nullable -> backfill values -> tighten to NOT NULL -> add the unique constraint. Skipping the nullable step on a non-empty table makes the ALTER fail (existing rows have NULL where NOT NULL is required). Doing the unique constraint before backfill works only on small tables; on large ones, build the index CONCURRENTLY in a separate step.

title: Faker-powered ArticleSeeder with relations — plan, build, verify (AI-resilient)
description:
Build an ArticleSeeder that uses @faker-js/faker to create 50 articles, each associated with 1 randomly chosen author and 1-3 randomly chosen tags from a pool of 10 pre-seeded tags. The seeder must use DatabaseSeeder as its root and be runnable via 'npx mikro-orm seeder:run'. Run it and verify with SELECT COUNT(*) FROM article and SELECT COUNT(*) FROM article_tags.

In the PR description, include: (1) the seed order — which entities must be created and flushed first and why, and what happens if you create an Article with a tag that has not been flushed yet; (2) the two COUNT(*) results proving it worked; (3) a critique — what would break if two developers ran the seeder on the same database simultaneously, and how you would make the seeder idempotent (e.g. em.upsert by natural key).

Submit the link to your branch or PR.
modelAnswer: Seed order: Tag and Author first (they have no required FKs), flush, then Article referencing them via em.getReference if you want to skip a SELECT. Without flushing tags first, an Article holding a Tag with id=undefined would fail at INSERT time. Concurrent runs collide on unique constraints (slug, tag.name) and produce partial duplicates; idempotency requires either upsert-by-natural-key (`em.upsert`) or a 'has this seeder run?' marker row. The deeper revelation: seeding is the cleanest way to feel why flush ordering is a dependency-aware topological sort, not just 'insert in the order I called create'.
